title: What I like: gustar
topic: gustar, encantar, interesar; the pronouns me, te, le, nos, os, les; también / tampoco
why: After the family and describing people, this lesson teaches you to say what you like with gustar, encantar and interesar, where the thing you like controls the verb. It introduces the pronouns me, te, le, nos, os, les and the reactions a mí también / tampoco, which you'll need in every conversation.

{"lessons": ["

Me gusta: the thing you like is in charge

Gustar doesn't work like “to like.” It works like “to be pleasing (to)”: Me gusta el café is literally “coffee is pleasing to me.” The subject of the verb is the thing you like; the person who likes it is a pronoun placed in front: me, te, le, nos, os, les.

The result: the verb doesn't agree with you, but with whatever is pleasing. One thing or one activity → gusta; several things → gustan.

EmphasisPronounOne thingSeveral things
(a mí)meme gusta el caféme gustan los libros
(a ti)tete gusta el caféte gustan los libros
(a él, a ella, a usted)lele gusta el caféle gustan los libros
(a nosotros, a nosotras)nosnos gusta el cafénos gustan los libros
(a vosotros, a vosotras)osos gusta el caféos gustan los libros
(a ellos, a ellas, a ustedes)lesles gusta el caféles gustan los libros

With a verb: always gusta

Before an infinitive, even if there are several, the verb stays singular: Me gusta bailar. Me gusta leer y escuchar música. Where English says “I like dancing” or “I like to dance,” Spanish uses the infinitive.

The article: unlike English

To talk about something in general, Spanish keeps the article, where English drops it: Me gusta el chocolate (I like chocolate), No me gustan las verduras (I don't like vegetables). The negative no goes right at the front: No me gusta.

Me gusta mucho la música, pero no me gustan los conciertos.I really like music, but I don't like concerts.

The trap: saying “yo gusto el café.” Yo gusto would mean “I am pleasing”! Always start with the pronoun: me gusta. And “I like it a lot” is never “me gusta muy”: it's me gusta mucho.

", "

A mí, a Lucía: emphasizing and clarifying

You can add a mí, a ti, a él… before the pronoun. It's like stressing the “I” in English: “I like it.” You're emphasizing or contrasting. But the little pronoun is still required: A mí me gusta, never “a mí gusta.”

A mí me gusta el mar, pero a mi hermano le gusta la montaña.I like the sea, but my brother likes the mountains.

Le and les are ambiguous (him, her, you). To be clear, name the person with a: A Pablo le gusta el fútbol. A mis padres les gusta viajar. Again, le or les stays in the sentence, even if it feels repetitive.

Verbs that work the same way

VerbMeaningExamples
encantarto love (things, activities)Me encanta la playa. Nos encantan las tapas.
interesarto interest¿Te interesa la historia? Me interesan los idiomas.
dolerto hurtMe duele la cabeza. Me duelen los pies.

Encantar is already very strong: “I love it” is simply me encanta. Doler changes its vowel like poder: remember me duele (one thing) and me duelen (several). With body parts, Spanish uses the article, not the possessive: Me duele la cabeza (my head hurts, I have a headache), not “mi cabeza.”

For anything interesting, fascinating or gripping, think interesar: Me interesa mucho el arte.

", "

A mí también, a mí tampoco

To react to someone's likes, Spanish has four short answers, matching English “me too,” “me neither,” “I do” and “I don't.”

Someone saysYou answerEnglish
Me gusta el cine.A mí también.Me too.
Me gusta el cine.A mí no.I don't. / Not me.
No me gusta el fútbol.A mí tampoco.Me neither.
No me gusta el fútbol.A mí sí.I do.

With gustar, the answer starts with a mí (not yo), since the person is the one “to whom it's pleasing.” With a normal verb, you keep yo: Vivo en Madrid. — Yo también.

— A mis hijos no les gustan las verduras. — A mi hija tampoco.— My kids don't like vegetables. — Neither does my daughter.

Asking

The question keeps the same word order, and only the intonation changes (no “do” needed): ¿Te gusta bailar? ¿A tu pareja le gusta cocinar? ¿Qué te gusta hacer los fines de semana?

Remember the logic: agreeing with a positive sentence → también; agreeing with a negative sentence → tampoco. Disagreeing → the opposite of the sentence: no after a positive, sí after a negative. Sí takes an accent when it means “yes” (or “I do”).
